title: We All Need Mentorship, Here's How to Make the Most of It
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart presents mentorship as a free and powerful form of professional development and gives a step-by-step approach to finding and keeping mentors. He starts with the disposition required, teachability that exceeds the urge to critique, and endorses Meenoo Rami's idea of many mentors playing distinct roles. He then walks through identifying potential mentors by asking, listening and observing, bringing them a specific question, actually doing what they advise, and following up with thanks. His own story of noticing a colleague's students writing better than his own anchors the advice. The post insists on authentic relationship over transactional networking and puts the burden of growth on the mentee's humility and follow-through.
points: Teachability, finding what could work in advice rather than what could not, is the precondition for being mentored.
A many-mentors mindset assigns different people different roles, from instructional fine-tuning to community to balance.
Mentors can be found by asking students and colleagues, listening to how teachers are described, and observing results.
Approach a prospective mentor with one specific question rather than asking them to be your mentor.
Acting on advice and following up with gratitude is what makes or breaks the relationship.
quotes: The key to growing from someone's mentorship is teachability, and teachability is about finding what could work in someone's advice rather than focusing on what couldn't.
Many schools have formal mentoring programs for new teachers, but these relationships aren't guaranteed to be authentic.
Our goal here isn't to check off our “Get a Mentor” box on the career to-do list; it's to cultivate a relationship with someone who 1) you respect and 2) will push you to grow in some way.
Instead, you simply ask them a specific question you're wrestling with. Ideally, this is 1) in person, and 2) related to what you've identified as their strength in Step 1.
Here's where you'll either make or break a mentoring relationship — you'll either act on a piece of advice they gave you, or you won't.
In most cases, and this is just a general observation of life, I find that people don't tend to value the advice they receive enough to actually try it out.
While you may not feel that you can offer your mentor much in terms of advice or guidance, the number one thing you must do for them is let them know that their advice wasn't a waste of their time.
